analysis.one_liner: Lets federal health officials test tobacco, disclose its additives and poisons, and restrict nicotine product marketing.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to force tobacco companies to disclose their additives and let federal officials test tar and nicotine levels died in the Senate Commerce Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have put tobacco products under the same federal food and drug law that covers other consumer products. Manufacturers would have to hand the government a complete list of every additive in their cigarettes and tobacco products, and the Secretary of Health and Human Services could ban or reduce any additive found unsafe. Before any brand could be sold, federal officials would have to test it and set its tar, nicotine, and carbon monoxide levels, and could make that information public; the bill also banned free samples and coupons for tobacco and regulated any non-tobacco nicotine product as a drug.
analysis.who_benefits: Smokers and the general public. Every brand of cigarette, chewing tobacco, and other tobacco product would have had its additives reported to the government and its tar, nicotine, and carbon monoxide levels federally tested and potentially disclosed, so consumers would finally know what was in the product and which brands carried higher levels of harmful constituents. If the Secretary found an additive unsafe, it could be reduced or banned outright. The bill also would have stopped free samples and coupon giveaways that draw new users into nicotine, and it would have treated any nicotine product outside the tobacco definition as a drug subject to drug law.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every tobacco manufacturer, importer, and packager to file a complete list of all additives used in their products, and lets the Secretary of Health and Human Services require public disclosure of those additives and ban or reduce any additive judged to present unnecessary increased risks to health.

Makes it unlawful to sell any tobacco brand until federal officials have tested it and established its tar, nicotine, carbon monoxide, and other harmful constituent levels, with the Secretary authorized to disclose that information to the public and to educate consumers that lower levels do not necessarily mean lower health risk.
Bans distributing tobacco as free samples or through coupons and other discount offers, closing off a marketing channel aimed at attracting new users.
Treats false or misleading tobacco advertising as grounds for declaring the product misbranded and illegal to distribute, adding a private-honesty standard on top of existing cigarette labeling laws.
Classifies any product containing nicotine that is not a tobacco product as a drug under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, closing a regulatory gap for non-tobacco nicotine delivery.
Directs the Secretary to report annually to Congress on tobacco additives, harmful constituent levels, and steps taken to reduce them, and to recommend further health protections.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers bear the direct costs: filing additive lists for every product, submitting to federal testing of every brand, possible reformulation if an additive is deemed unsafe, and losing free-sample and coupon marketing. Some compliance costs would likely be passed on to smokers through higher prices, and tobacco advertisers and promoters lose a channel for discount-based promotion. The bill's own findings note tobacco costs the country more than $60 billion a year in lost productivity and health care costs, a burden the regulation was meant to shrink.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs on manufacturers — additive filings, testing of every brand, and possible reformulation — would likely be passed to consumers as higher cigarette prices, which falls partly on the smokers the bill is trying to protect.

The bill leaves the core product legal; the Secretary could restrict additives and require disclosure but could not ban cigarettes themselves, and the bill itself concedes that reduced levels of tar, nicotine, or carbon monoxide do not necessarily mean reduced health risk.

Giving one cabinet secretary authority to require reduced or prohibited additive levels, with labeling and information mandates set by regulation, concentrates significant discretion in an unelected agency, a standard objection to expanding the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act's reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is substantial by the bill's own findings: tobacco was the single most preventable cause of death in the United States, cost over $60 billion a year in lost productivity and health care, and remained one of the least regulated consumer products, with an industry spending more than $2 billion a year to promote it. The costs — manufacturer compliance, some price pass-through, and loss of sampling and coupon marketing — are real but modest against that scale, and the disclosure provisions cost the public nothing but give them information they did not have. The main design weakness is that the bill stops short of restricting the product itself and relies on disclosure, which does not by itself reduce harm.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in April 1989 and sent to the Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Bingaman introduced the bill on April 13, 1989 with Senator Bill Bradley and Senator John Chafee, giving it sponsorship from both parties, and it was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
Three senators cosponsored the bill in total — 2 of 55 Senate Democrats and 1 of 45 Senate Republicans.
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 with the bill still sitting in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers came out ahead: they avoided federal additive disclosure, government testing of tar and nicotine levels for every brand, and restrictions on free samples and coupons, and consumers went without the ingredient information the bill would have provided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies that avoided federal oversight

for.name: Jeff Bingaman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it to the Commerce Committee.

for.name: John Chafee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Daniel Inouye (D-HI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on April 13, 1989 and never reported it out, held no recorded action on it, and it never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The industry of the era opposed federal health-and-safety regulation of tobacco, which the bill would have imposed for the first time; its opposition was public and well covered.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was small but bipartisan — 2 of 55 Senate Democrats and 1 of 45 Senate Republicans — and because the bill never got a vote, no partisan split on the merits was ever recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have forced cigarette and smokeless tobacco makers to file complete additive lists with the government, submit every brand to federal testing of tar, nicotine, and carbon monoxide levels, accept possible bans on unsafe additives, and give up free-sample and coupon marketing. Their interest in avoiding disclosure and testing ran directly against the public's interest in knowing what is in the product.

The bill declares false tobacco advertising a form of misbranding and outlaws free samples and coupon discounts, cutting into the more than $2 billion a year the bill's findings say the industry spends promoting its products.
